scenes.name: hook
scenes.text: Some people hear again with a small device behind the ear. But hearing aids and cochlear implants work in very different ways.

scenes.name: ear
scenes.text: Sound makes the eardrum vibrate. Deep inside, the cochlea has thousands of tiny hair cells that turn vibrations into nerve signals.

scenes.name: aid
scenes.text: A hearing aid has a microphone, a tiny processor, and a speaker. It makes sounds louder, so weakened hair cells can still pick them up.

scenes.name: tune
scenes.text: It's programmed from your hearing test, boosting only the pitches you struggle with, not everything equally.

scenes.name: implant
scenes.text: When hair cells are badly damaged, louder sound doesn't help. A cochlear implant skips them completely.

scenes.name: electrodes
scenes.text: An outer processor sends coded sound through the skin to the implant, which drives a thin row of electrodes inside the cochlea, stimulating the hearing nerve directly.

scenes.name: learn
scenes.text: It needs surgery, and the brain takes time to learn these new signals. With practice, many people understand speech again.

scenes.name: outro
scenes.text: Amplify, or bypass. Two ways back to sound. Follow for more on how things really work.
